title: Mental Maths for Grade 1: What Your Child Can Really Do (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: Mental Maths for Grade 1 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: The mental maths a Grade 1 child can really do: number bonds, counting on, making ten and doubles, plus a daily routine and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Mental maths in Grade 1 is not about speed drills. It is a handful of thinking tricks — number bonds, counting on, making ten, doubles — that let a six-year-old add without fingers. Here is what to teach, in what order.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
When a parent tells me their six-year-old is ‘bad at mental maths’, I usually find the opposite is true — the child is doing plenty of mental work, just slowly and on their fingers. Mental maths in Grade 1 is not a race to blurt out answers. It is a small set of thinking tricks that let a child add and subtract inside their head instead of counting every single time. Get those tricks in the right order and the speed follows on its own.

So what can a Grade 1 child realistically do in their head? More than most parents expect. Below are the four mental maths skills I would build first, why the order matters, and a ten-minute daily routine that actually fits a school-night. No apps, no flashcard marathons — just a handful of counters and a bit of patience.

What mental maths looks like at the Grade 1 level

The NCERT Grade 1 maths goal is confident addition and subtraction within 20, moving away from counting-all. Mental maths is the ‘moving away’ part. A child who reasons ‘8 and 5 — that is 10 and 3, so 13’ is doing mental maths. A child who counts thirteen fingers to get there is not yet. Both reach 13; only one has a method that will still work in Grade 3.

Here is the honest bit: do not chase speed in Grade 1. A child who thinks through 8 + 5 in four seconds is in a far stronger place than one who has rote-memorised it but cannot explain why. Understanding first, speed later.

1. Number bonds — the foundation everything sits on

If I could teach only one mental maths skill in Grade 1, it would be number bonds to ten: the pairs that make ten — 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5. A child who knows these cold finds the rest of primary arithmetic easier for years.

Use a ten-frame — two rows of five squares. Put four counters in it and ask ‘how many more to fill it?’ Do this daily for a couple of weeks until the answer comes without counting. The point is not memorising ten facts; it is seeing that 4 and 6 belong together, so 6 + 4, 10 − 4 and 10 − 6 are all the same picture. One bond, four facts.

2. Counting on from the bigger number

Most children start by counting all: for 3 + 5 they count out three, then five, then start again from one. Counting on is the first real leap — keep the bigger number in your head and count up from it. For 3 + 5, start at 5 and go ‘six, seven, eight.’

Always start from the bigger number. Adding 2 + 9 by counting on from 2 is nine hops; from 9 it is two. Children genuinely enjoy noticing that 2 + 9 and 9 + 2 land in the same spot. That idea — order does not matter in addition — is a Grade 1 milestone by itself, and it halves the counting.

3. Making ten to cross the ten-line

This is the strategy that finally retires the fingers, and it is the most powerful mental maths move a Grade 1 child learns. To add 8 + 5, borrow 2 from the 5 to complete the 8 into 10, then add the leftover 3: 8 + 5 becomes 10 + 3 = 13. It leans directly on number bonds, which is exactly why bonds come first.

It feels like a stretch at the start. Model it out loud with counters and a ten-frame for about a week before expecting a child to do it alone. Once it clicks, sums that used to be scary — 7 + 6, 9 + 4 — become quick head-work.

4. Doubles and near-doubles

Children pick up doubles — 3 + 3, 4 + 4, 5 + 5 — surprisingly happily, maybe because they sound like a chant. Once doubles are secure, near-doubles come almost free: 6 + 7 is just double 6 and one more. Teaching 6 + 7 as ‘double 6, plus 1’ is far kinder than counting on seven times.

How the skills fit together

Mental maths skillBest forWorked example
Number bonds to 10Anything that makes ten7 + 3 = 10
Counting onA small second number6 + 2 = 8
Making tenCrossing ten (sum 11–18)8 + 5 = 13
Doubles / near-doublesEqual or almost-equal numbers7 + 8 = 15

A ten-minute daily routine that works

Ten focused minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday. A pattern that has worked well for parents I know in Tier-2 cities where after-school time is short:

  • Mon & Tue: ten-frame bonds to ten — ‘how many more to fill it?’
  • Wed & Thu: making ten with counters, said out loud
  • Fri: a quick doubles chant, then near-doubles
  • Weekend: mixed written practice, so the child has to choose a method rather than being told which one

That choosing step on the weekend is where real fluency shows up. When a child looks at 9 + 4 and decides on their own to make ten, the mental maths has landed.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Mental Maths Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on number bonds, counting on, making ten and doubles. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: 3 and 7 fill a ten-frame exactly. The bonds to ten are 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 and 5+5.

questions.q: What is 5 + 3, counting on from the bigger number?
questions.explanation: Start at 5 and count on three: 6, 7, 8.
Take 2 from the 5 to turn 8 into 10, then add the leftover 3. 10 + 3 = 13.
This is a double. Double 6 is 12.

questions.q: 6 + 7 is the same as which of these?
questions.explanation: 6 + 7 is a near-double: double 6 is 12, and one more makes 13.

questions.q: Which sum gives the same answer as 2 + 9?
questions.explanation: Order does not matter in addition, so 2 + 9 and 9 + 2 both equal 11.

questions.q: How many more counters fill a ten-frame that already has 4?
questions.explanation: 4 and 6 make ten, so 6 more counters fill the frame.

questions.q: A child has 9 sweets and is given 4 more. Using make ten, how many now?
questions.explanation: Take 1 from the 4 to turn 9 into 10, then add the leftover 3. 10 + 3 = 13.

faq.q: What mental maths should a Grade 1 child be able to do?
faq.a: By the end of Grade 1 the aim is addition and subtraction within 20 using strategies — number bonds to ten, counting on, making ten and doubles — rather than counting on fingers every time. Fluent recall of bonds to ten is the key marker.

faq.q: How is mental maths different from just memorising sums?
faq.a: Memorising gives one fact at a time. A child who understands the bond 4 and 6 also knows 6 + 4, 10 − 4 and 10 − 6 — and can rebuild the answer if they forget. Understanding is more reliable than rote, and it transfers to bigger numbers later.

faq.q: Is it a problem if my child still counts on fingers?
faq.a: Not at the start — fingers make the maths concrete. The goal is to give better tools, especially making ten, so the child chooses to leave fingers behind. Banning fingers before offering a replacement just causes stress.

faq.q: How much daily mental maths practice is enough?
faq.a: About ten focused minutes a day, mixing one strategy drill with a few spoken or written questions, beats a long weekly session. Consistency matters far more than length at this age.
